concepts.name: Composables must be free of side effects
Network security config defaults: cleartext and trust anchors

questions.prompt: A composable declares `var items = 0`, runs `items++` inside the `for` loop that emits each `Card`, then shows `Text("Count: $items")`. Why does the count come out wrong?

choices.text: Composables can run in any order and as often as every frame, so writes repeat
The slot table resets every local `var` to its first value before each new frame
`items` must be a `mutableStateOf(0)`, so Compose can observe every increment
Each `Card` lambda already runs on a background thread, so the increments race

questions.explanation: The Compose mental model guide uses this exact bug: composables and their lambdas can run in any order, may recompose on their own, and can rerun as often as every frame, so a write to a shared variable during composition gives a wrong count. Making `items` a `mutableStateOf` doesn't help: it is still a write during composition, which the docs say never to do. Composables don't run in parallel today; the rule exists so Compose could do that later.

sources.title: Thinking in Compose
sources.claim: The guide's `ListWithBug` example shows `items++` inside a composable displaying the wrong count, because composables can execute in any order, may run as often as every frame, and writes like this are not supported; composables cannot currently run in parallel.

sources.title: Follow best practices (Compose performance)
sources.claim: You can avoid backwards writes altogether by never writing to state in Composition; write to state in response to an event, in a lambda such as `onClick`.

questions.prompt: Your app targets API 35 and must load images from one legacy host that only serves `http://`. Every other call uses HTTPS. What is the narrowest change that works?

choices.text: Set `cleartextTrafficPermitted="true"` on `base-config`, which then covers every host
Nothing: cleartext is allowed until the app declares a network security config file
Add a `domain-config` for that one host with `cleartextTrafficPermitted="true"`
List the host under `debug-overrides`, whose settings also apply to release builds

questions.explanation: Apps targeting Android 9 (API 28) or higher get a default `base-config` with `cleartextTrafficPermitted="false"`, so the `http://` call is refused even with no config file. A `domain-config` scoped to the one host re-allows cleartext there and nowhere else; changing `base-config` would also work but allows HTTP to every host. `debug-overrides` is ignored entirely when the app isn't debuggable, which is the case for release builds.

sources.title: Network security configuration
sources.claim: The default configuration for apps targeting Android 9 (API 28) and higher has `base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false"` trusting system CAs; `domain-config` sets cleartextTrafficPermitted per domain; `debug-overrides` is completely ignored when `android:debuggable` is false.

questions.prompt: A manifest-declared `BroadcastReceiver` uploads a log file from `onReceive()`. You see broadcast ANRs, and when you move the upload to a new thread some uploads never finish. Explain both problems and how you would fix them.

model_answer.summary: `onReceive()` runs on the main thread under an ANR timeout, and once it returns the process may be killed, so a bare thread is unsafe; `goAsync()` only buys time until the same timeout, so long work belongs in a scheduled job.
key_points: `onReceive()` runs on the main thread and must finish within the broadcast timeout (10 seconds for a foreground broadcast on Android 13 and lower, 10-20 seconds on 14+, longer for background broadcasts), so a slow upload there causes an ANR
After `onReceive()` returns, the system may kill a process that only hosts a manifest-declared receiver, so a thread started there can die before the upload finishes
`goAsync()` keeps the broadcast active and lets the work move off the main thread, but `PendingResult.finish()` must be called on every path, within the same timeout
Long work such as an upload should be scheduled as a job (JobScheduler, or a library on top of it) instead of running inside the receiver

questions.explanation: Broadcast receivers are meant for small, quick work. Spawning a thread looks like the fix for the ANR, but it trades it for lost work, since the receiver's process has low importance once `onReceive()` returns. `goAsync()` is still bound by the timeout (the docs say the system expects you to finish in under 10 seconds), so it suits short async work, not an upload.

sources.title: Broadcasts overview
sources.claim: `onReceive()` runs on the main thread and should return quickly; the system can kill a process hosting only a manifest-declared receiver after `onReceive()` returns; `goAsync()` keeps the broadcast active but the system still expects you to finish within 10 seconds, and long work should be scheduled with JobScheduler.

sources.title: Diagnose and fix ANRs
sources.claim: Broadcast timeouts are 10 seconds (foreground) and 60 seconds (background) on Android 13 and lower and 10-20 or 60-120 seconds on Android 14+; with `goAsync()` a timeout means `PendingResult.finish()` was not called in time, and forgetting `finish()` on a code path is a common cause.

questions.prompt: A list row calls `analytics.logImpression(item.id)` directly in its composable body, to log each item once when it is shown. Why is this unreliable?

choices.text: Strong Skipping skips every non-composable call, so the impression is never logged
Compose runs a composable body only once, at first composition, and never again
The compiler rejects it, as composable bodies may only call other composables
Recomposition can rerun or be canceled, so it logs repeats or for UI never shown

questions.explanation: A composable body can run many times, as often as every frame, and recomposition is optimistic: Compose may cancel it and discard the UI tree, but a side effect already applied stays applied. So logging from the body double-counts and can log rows the user never saw. Run such work in an effect handler such as `LaunchedEffect` keyed on the item, or from an event.

sources.title: Thinking in Compose
sources.claim: Recomposition is optimistic and may be canceled, discarding the UI tree while side effects already applied remain; composable functions might run as often as every frame; updating shared objects or observables is a dangerous side effect.

questions.prompt: A QA tester installs a proxy's CA certificate as a user certificate to inspect your release build's HTTPS traffic. The app targets API 35 and has no network security config. What happens?

choices.text: The app trusts it, since every installed CA is trusted unless pinning is configured
The app trusts it only if the tester also sets the app's debuggable flag in Settings
The app still trusts only system CAs by default, so the proxied connections fail
The app trusts it for cleartext HTTP but rejects it for any connection over HTTPS

questions.explanation: Since Android 7.0 (API 24), apps by default trust only the system CA store; user-added CAs are trusted by default only for apps targeting API 23 or lower. To inspect traffic in development, add the proxy CA under `debug-overrides`, which applies only when the app is debuggable and is ignored in release builds.

sources.title: Network security configuration
sources.claim: Default configurations trust only `system` certificates for apps targeting API 24 and higher, and `system` plus `user` certificates only for API 23 and lower; `debug-overrides` trust anchors apply only when `android:debuggable` is true.

questions.prompt: A receiver calls `goAsync()` and passes the `PendingResult` to a worker thread. One error path returns without calling `finish()`. What happens when that path runs?

choices.text: The broadcast times out, and the app gets a broadcast receiver ANR
Nothing: the system calls `finish()` once `onReceive()` has returned
The broadcast is delivered again the next time the process starts up
Only a logcat warning, since an ANR can come from the main thread only

questions.explanation: For a receiver that calls `goAsync()`, the broadcast timeout means `PendingResult.finish()` wasn't called in time, and a missing `finish()` on some code path is one of the documented causes of broadcast ANRs. The work being on a worker thread doesn't exempt it: the same timeout applies as for a synchronous receiver.

sources.title: Diagnose and fix ANRs
sources.claim: For async receivers that call `goAsync()`, a broadcast ANR means `PendingResult.finish()` wasn't called in time; 'Forgot to call PendingResult.finish' is a listed cause, and `finish()` is subject to the same timeout as synchronous receivers.

questions.prompt: A manifest-declared `BroadcastReceiver` uploads a log file in `onReceive()` and causes broadcast ANRs; moving the upload to a new thread makes some uploads never finish. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: `onReceive()` runs on the main thread, so a slow upload there can cause an ANR
`goAsync()` lifts the broadcast timeout, so the upload may take as long as needed
Once `onReceive()` returns, the system may kill the process, ending the thread
A plain thread started in `onReceive()` keeps the process alive until it ends
With `goAsync()`, `PendingResult.finish()` must be called on every code path

questions.explanation: `onReceive()` runs on the main thread and must finish within the broadcast timeout, so a slow upload there causes an ANR. Once it returns, the system may kill a process that only hosts a manifest-declared receiver, and a bare thread doesn't keep it alive. `goAsync()` moves the work off the main thread, but the timeout still runs until `PendingResult.finish()` is called, so call it on every path and keep the work short (about 10 seconds). Schedule long work such as an upload as a job instead.

sources.title: Broadcasts overview
sources.claim: `onReceive()` runs on the main thread; the system may kill the process right after `onReceive()` returns for a manifest-declared receiver, so don't start long-running threads there; `goAsync()` suits work under about 10 seconds and needs `PendingResult.finish()`, and longer work should be scheduled with JobScheduler.

sources.title: Diagnose and fix ANRs
sources.claim: Broadcast timeouts are 10 seconds (foreground) and 60 seconds (background) on Android 13 and lower, and 10-20 or 60-120 seconds on Android 14+; for a `goAsync()` receiver the timeout runs until `PendingResult.finish()` is called, so always call `finish()` on all code paths.
